This paper presents a unique dataset featuring 15-minute recordings of birds in a residential setting within the Baltimore area, accompanied by manual annotations of birdsong and background noise. We also outline the steps for annotating audio files containing birdsong and ambient sounds. Additionally, we demonstrate the potential of using this dataset to train machine learning models capable of distinguishing birdsong from other audio elements.

We introduce a novel neural network-based image reconstruction approach for
event cameras that significantly simplifies the event camera calibration process.
Our method leverages a trained neural network to reconstruct image pixels from
raw events, eliminating the need for extensive target capture and ground truth
labeling. This method is versatile, applicable to both initial camera
calibration and subsequent target-based calibration. We demonstrate its
effectiveness in achieving accurate target-based calibration with minimal
targets across various resolutions and scenarios.

Graph learning involves working with data represented as graphs, which have become increasingly prominent in the field of machine learning. However, the theoretical understanding of graph learning remains incomplete, particularly when it comes to its relationship with traditional tabular data. Unlike tabular data, which can be viewed as a type of graph, the theoretical properties of graph learning models are not yet fully understood. In this study, we investigate the theoretical properties of graph learning by introducing a new framework that views the data as a type of graph. We have established a theoretical framework for graph learning and have shown that it can be viewed as a type of generalized linear regression. Our research also explores the generalization error of graph learning and has identified key factors that influence its performance, including the structure of the data and the choice of learning algorithm. Our findings provide new insights into the theoretical properties of graph learning and have the potential to guide the development of new algorithms for this type of data.

We provide an in-depth categorization of exceptional curves on a specific type of K3 surface known as a weak del Pezzo surface. This classification is achieved through utilizing the Mordell--Weil group of a generic self-mirroring map derived from the surface. Consequently, our findings enable us to identify all possible exceptional divisors on a weak del Pezzo surface, and we demonstrate that the set of such divisors is indeed a variable in a specific set of divisors on a generic del Pezzo surface of degree 1.

This study introduces a novel image-guided approach for robot-assisted retinal surgery, enhancing the precision and efficiency of intraocular procedures. The proposed system leverages a 3D reconstruction of the eye to provide a surgeon with a comprehensive, 3D view of the surgical site. To achieve this, we developed a method for creating a 3D model of the eye using a combination of camera images and a pre-existing 2D image. The model is then utilized to guide the surgeon's instrument to the target area. To ensure the surgeon's control over the robot, we implemented a real-time tracking system to monitor the instrument's movement. The proposed method was tested using a simulated environment and a real-world setup, demonstrating its effectiveness in generating a 3D model and tracking the instrument in real-time. The results of the study provide a foundation for the development of a fully automated image-guided robot-assisted retinal surgery system.

This paper extends the findings of Bridgeland and Guo by examining the $F$-polynomials of rank 2 in the quantum torus associated with type $A_{n}$ or $D_{n}$-quivers and determines their coefficients. We also investigate the potential to generalize these results to higher rank quivers.

The WebAuthn standard has been widely adopted, allowing web developers to leverage various physical and biometric authentication methods, such as smart cards, fingerprint readers, and USB security keys. This has led to a significant increase in the use of second-factor authentication on the web. Despite its benefits, there remains debate over whether it is feasible to eventually phase out passwords entirely from web authentication. This study investigates the adoption of WebAuthn among top websites, their respective security practices, and the types of devices used by visitors to access these sites. Our analysis reveals that, while Webauthn is becoming more popular, there remains a significant reliance on passwords for authentication.

A common technique used to analyze the behavior of particles in discrete lattice models involves replacing their momentum with a continuous range of momentum values derived from the lattice's reciprocal space. However, this approach has a significant limitation, as it does not allow for the consideration of momentum values that are not exactly integer multiples of the lattice's fundamental unit. This paper proposes a new method for generalizing the momentum of particles to include non-integer values that are still rational numbers. This expansion is achieved by redefining the relationship between momentum and energy in the Schrödinger equation, and subsequently deriving a new set of momentum eigenfunctions. The paper then demonstrates the feasibility of this approach through its application to the harmonic oscillator and the kicked harmonic oscillator.

The widespread adoption of video streaming apps on mobile devices has led to a significant impact on our daily routines and leisure activities. These apps have become an essential part of our lives, providing a constant supply of entertainment and educational content. However, the design of these apps often prioritizes engagement over user preferences, resulting in features like autoplay that can be frustrating and lead to excessive screen time. In this study, we examine the effects of autoplay on user behavior and well-being, and how the removal of this feature affects the user experience in a popular video app. Our research reveals that removing autoplay enables users to have more control over their content consumption, resulting in improved satisfaction and reduced screen time. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the app's design can influence user agency, with autoplay having a negative impact on user satisfaction and overall well-being.

We have established that every behavior exhibited by a reactive Turing machine with infinite data can be approximated by a finitely executable behavior displayed by a related reactive Turing machine with finite data. This finding validates Zeno Klin's conjecture.

A combinatorial Gray code is a systematic, orderless sequence of objects, 
where each object differs from its predecessor in a single, distinct way. 
In this study, we develop a Gray code for ordered trees with three kinds of 
modifications: adding a leaf, removing a leaf, and adjusting an internal edge. 
We also investigate the resulting sequence's properties, including its 
avoidance of consecutive objects with the same number of edges, and its 
combinatorial efficiency.

The sPHENIX experiment at RHIC is poised to explore the high-energy nuclear physics landscape with its cutting-edge detector and data acquisition system. This comprehensive report details the crucial components of sPHENIX, including its design, simulated performance, and computing infrastructure, outlining the intricate processes behind data analysis and storage.

This study introduces a novel finite element approach for analyzing dynamic problems in space-time domains that are undergoing shape changes. The proposed method leverages the capabilities of the Discontinuous Galerkin Spectral Element Method and incorporates several key enhancements. These improvements include a space-time approach to mesh construction, a novel polynomial basis, and a novel numerical flux formulation. The proposed method ensures that the discretized space-time slabs are conforming, enabling efficient handling of changing domains. Additionally, the method allows for the integration of various mesh deformation techniques, such as those based on Lagrangian or Eulerian meshes, and can be used in conjunction with arbitrary mesh interpolation methods. The proposed method is demonstrated through several numerical examples, including a 1D wave equation problem and 2D and 3D problems modeling material deformation and real-world applications.

In a signed graph, the circular flow index is the maximum number of arcs in an odd cycle that has an alternating sign. We derive upper bounds for the circular flow index of specific types of signed graphs, including those with particular restrictions on the sign distribution.

We investigate the computational complexity of the Modular Subset Sum problem within the context of complexity theory. Specifically, we focus on a modified version of this problem, referred to as the $(a,b)$- Modular Subset Sum problem, where we are given a set of $n$ positive integers, $b$ positive integers, and a target value $a$. Our objective is to determine whether it is possible to select $b$ elements from the given set such that their sum equals $a$. To this end, we develop a Monte-Carlo randomized algorithm that can solve this problem in $O(n\log^2 n)$ time, and we also provide a deterministic algorithm that can solve it in $O(n\log n)$ time. Furthermore, we prove that this problem is unlikely to have a randomized algorithm that can solve it in subquadratic time.

We have conducted a study of stellar flares occurring on nearby M dwarfs, which were observed using the 2.56-m Nordic Optical Telescope at La Palma. Our analysis of the flares' characteristics, such as their energy levels, durations, and temperatures, revealed some interesting patterns. Specifically, we found that flares on the order of magnitude of ergs exhibit a range of durations, and their temperatures tend to be higher than those of non-flaring stars. Furthermore, we discovered that the flares' durations are correlated with their energies, and the flares' temperatures are similar to those of the non-flaring stars. Our findings also suggest that the flares' emission lines are broadened due to the flares' high temperatures and the Doppler broadening caused by the stars' rotation. Our research provides valuable insights into the properties of stellar flares and their host stars.

During the early stages of Drosophila melanogaster embryogenesis, crucial processes such as morphogenesis and immune response are facilitated by hemocytes, a type of immune cell. These cells are dispersed throughout the embryo and play a pivotal role in the immune response, however, the precise locations of hemocytes within the embryo are not readily available. To address this, researchers have developed a new method that leverages the embryo's morphological features to accurately identify and localize hemocytes. This method involves utilizing a deep learning approach, specifically a convolutional neural network, to analyze the embryo's morphology and identify the correct hemocyte locations. The developed method demonstrates high accuracy, with a 0.95 F1 score, and has been successfully applied to a large dataset of Drosophila embryos.

This study introduces a new approach to speech recognition through a contrastive
siamese network, which aims to reduce the reliance on extensive labeled data.
The model comprises two main components: a backbone network and a contrastive
module. The backbone network is trained on a limited set of labeled data, and the
contrastive module is trained to distinguish between audio inputs and their
unlabeled counterparts. The model's ability to generalize to new, unlabeled data
is then evaluated using a speech recognition task. The proposed method is
experimentally applied to the LibriSpeech dataset, and the results indicate a
notable improvement in speech recognition accuracy when supplemented with
unlabeled data.

A new scaling variable $\xi_w$ has been proposed for the description of the $F_2$ structure function and neutrino-nucleon scattering cross sections. This variable, based on the $x$-dependence of the parton distribution functions, allows for a unified treatment of both particle and deep inelastic scattering processes at small $x$. Using the GLAP equations, an analytical expression for the structure function $F_2$ has been derived in terms of $\xi_w$. This expression, combined with the $Q^2$-evolution of the parton distribution functions, enables a comprehensive, multi-process analysis of the structure function data. The results of this analysis, incorporating data from HERA and the Tevatron, demonstrate the effectiveness of the $\xi_w$ variable in accurately describing the structure function and cross section data across a broad range of $x$ and $Q^2$.

This study explores the fundamental characteristics of adaptive control systems governed by stochastic differential equations, with a focus on the mathematical and computational aspects. The research reveals that the resulting process is regular only when unmeasurable states are directly linked to the control mechanism used, which involves a combination of deterministic and Gaussian noise. Furthermore, the system exhibits a unique property where the expected value of the system's trajectory, influenced by unknown parameters, can be precisely calculated. The results are also applicable to cases involving feedback controls based on observations, provided that the control mechanism is directly linked to the observed states. Notably, the system's expected value can be determined using a combination of deterministic and Gaussian noise, even in cases involving unobservable feedback controls. The research also examines the system's behavior over a finite time period and finds that the expected value of the system's trajectory, influenced by unknown parameters, can be precisely calculated. The results are further illustrated through numerical examples, which demonstrate the practical applications of the theoretical findings.

A new theory, active inference, offers a comprehensive brain theory that links
various brain areas and behaviors to a core principle: organisms try to minimize
surprise in their environment through constant learning. This framework has been
extended to account for the complexities of branching time, where multiple future
outcomes are possible, but its new version, branching time active inference (BTAI),
suffers from instability issues in certain scenarios, such as grid cell simulations.
This paper investigates the causes of these stability problems and proposes a
solution by introducing a new constraint that prevents the emergence of unbounded
complexity in the model. This modification allows for the successful simulation
of grid cell dynamics, enabling a deeper understanding of the neural mechanisms
behind this phenomenon.

We have developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic model that describes the quark gluon plasma's response to a sudden increase in baryon density. This model is based on a previously established model for the quark plasma, with the addition of a specific term to account for baryons. We have shown that this model is mathematically consistent and can be simplified to a more manageable form under specific conditions. Our model predicts that a pulse of baryon density will propagate through the quark gluon plasma without losing energy, and will eventually lead to a separation of baryons and quarks. This prediction is consistent with experimental data from the relativistic heavy ion collider.

We show that a particular type of space, specifically those with a certain topology where every point has a countable neighborhood, have the property of being Eberlein-Grothendieck when the functions that map each point to its values on that point form a particular kind of vector space. Furthermore, we establish that a space with a certain kind of vector structure, where every point has a topologically compact set associated with it, is Eberlein-Grothendieck if and only if it meets a particular criterion regarding compactness.

We provide the necessary conditions for isochronicity in a Hamiltonian system with a single degree of freedom. These conditions are more inclusive than those established by Poincaré, allowing for both periodic and constant solutions. Additionally, we demonstrate the application of these conditions in two specific cases: the Poincaré-Cartan system and the Hill-type Hamiltonian.

We have developed a new approach to analyzing complex dynamic systems by introducing a similarity signature curve, which leverages the similarity between orbits in phase space and provides a more efficient representation of chaotic behavior. This approach is applied to the widely studied Lorenz system and we demonstrate its utility by using it to identify key parameters that influence the system's behavior, including the Rabinovich-Quinn parameter, and to identify the onset of chaos in parameter space.
This paper examines the LAN property of a statistical model for a continuous-time Markov-modulated Hawkes process with a general intensity function.

For Laplacians on non-self-adjoint vector bundles over compact hyperbolic surfaces with a non-trivial structure, we establish that the spectral set satisfies Weyl's law at a half-integral spectrum level. This result is extended to the non-self-adjoint analog of cusp Laplacians on non-trivial vector bundles over compact arithmetic surfaces with a non-trivial structure.

This study introduces FNetAR, a causal language model variant of the recently proposed FNet model, which employs additive instead of multiplicative attention. We also developed an optimized version of FNetAR that leverages self-referential attention, resulting in significantly reduced computational requirements. Our experiments on the causal language modeling benchmark demonstrate that FNetAR outperforms the Transformer-XL baseline with a notable improvement of 0.28% in perplexity and exhibit comparable results to other state-of-the-art models like Longformer and BigBird.

In this research, we investigate the behavior of the universe in an interacting dark energy model where the energy density of the universe is influenced by a time-dependent interaction parameter. We examine the universe's evolution in the presence of a decaying dark matter component with a specific interaction mechanism. We analyze the universe's dynamics using both analytical and numerical methods, focusing on the universe's transition from a deceleration to an acceleration phase. We also investigate the evolution of the Hubble parameter and the deceleration parameter in the context of the interacting dark energy model.

This study focuses on optimizing service function chaining (SFC) at the network edge by integrating multiple SFC requests into a shared edge node. A novel game theory-based approach is proposed to balance the needs of users and edge network resources by incorporating edge selection and SFC path mapping. The approach utilizes non-cooperative game theory to optimize SFC path mapping and edge selection, ensuring the convergence of the two games. A theoretical analysis confirms the stability of the Nash equilibrium in both games. Experimental results demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed approach in improving network utility and reducing edge load.

In two-dimensional disordered superconductors, a phase transition occurs between a diffusive thermal metal and a topological superconductor state. We investigate the nature of this transition in the presence of a small external magnetic field. Our analysis reveals that the transition point is characterized by a unique, stable combination of values for two critical exponents. As the temperature increases, this transition becomes more pronounced and occurs at a lower external magnetic field.

This study delves into the complex dynamics of depression, a mental health issue affecting a significant portion of the global population. Depression is characterized by persistent feelings of sadness and a lack of interest in daily activities, often accompanied by a distorted perception of reality. Researchers have found that social media can be a valuable tool in detecting depression, as it provides a window into an individual's daily thoughts and feelings. Building on this idea, our research explores the relationship between depression and the concept of happiness on social media. We propose that depression can be linked to an overemphasis on happiness, as individuals struggling with depression often compare their own happiness to the idealized happiness presented in social media. Our study uses a large dataset of tweets from depressed users, and we find that depression can be detected by analyzing the balance between tweets about happiness and tweets about sadness.

The universe's mysterious dark matter, comprising approximately 27% of its total mass, has been a long-standing enigma in astrophysics. Despite its presence being confirmed, little is known about its composition, with various hypothetical particles such as WIMPs, sterile neutrinos, and axions being proposed. This article provides an overview of the latest advancements in dark matter research, both theoretically and observationally. We begin by examining the universe's dark matter, followed by an exploration of the theoretical frameworks that aim to explain its composition. Next, we discuss the observational evidence for dark matter, both in the universe at large and in the formation of galaxies and clusters. This discussion is followed by an in-depth examination of the most promising methods for detecting dark matter, both in the universe and in the laboratory. Finally, we conclude with a summary of the key findings and unresolved challenges in dark matter research.

A new type of triangular antiferromagnetic order has been identified in the compound Na$_{4-\delta}$Ni$^{2+}$TeO$_{6}$ at temperatures below approximately 20 K. This finding is consistent with theoretical predictions for triangular antiferromagnets and is supported by specific heat measurements showing a unique spin structure. Furthermore, the compound exhibits a characteristic temperature-dependent shift in its X-ray diffraction patterns, which is attributed to a possible spin-liquid to triangular antiferromagnetic phase transition.

The widespread adoption of IoT devices has led to the development of innovative applications that rely on trust management to ensure the integrity of IoT networks. However, the presence of uncertain data sources compromises the reliability of trust, which can result in the loss of trust due to inaccurate measurements and conflicting opinions among devices. This research focuses on the development of a trust management framework that leverages machine learning to address the challenges associated with uncertain data in IoT networks. The proposed framework incorporates a trust evaluation mechanism that utilizes a neural network to predict trust, and a learning algorithm that updates trust ratings based on the performance of the prediction model. The framework also includes a recovery mechanism that ensures the trustworthiness of the IoT network in the event of a prediction error. The research evaluates the effectiveness of the proposed framework using a simulation-based approach, and the results demonstrate its superiority over existing trust management frameworks.

This study delves into the Gibbs phenomenon's impact on spline interpolation. It specifically examines two methods: univariate cubic spline interpolation and a multivariate approach using linear cubic splines for 3D image reconstruction. The research aims to determine the necessary sample density for the reconstruction process to be stable, with regards to both spatial and color aspects.

This study examines four-dimensional Taub-NUT spacetimes within the context of Einstein-$\Lambda$ theory through a Hamiltonian constrained approach. The analysis yields a wide range of solutions, encompassing asymptotically flat spacetimes like the Taub-NUT-Bolt solution, asymptotically de Sitter spacetimes, and asymptotically anti-de Sitter spacetimes, as well as asymptotically flat cosmologies. Notably, the research also identifies a Taub-NUT spacetime with a closed, non-flat universe. The analysis of the cosmological solutions reveals that the spacetime contains a black hole, and a conformal flat, non-compact spacetime with a closed universe. The study further investigates the thermodynamic properties of the cosmological solutions, including the cosmological constant, and demonstrates that the first law of thermodynamics holds for these spacetimes. The analysis also shows that the cosmological solutions conform to the Smarr formula, and that the thermodynamic quantities exhibit a scaling behavior with respect to the Taub-NUT charge.

Accurate multimedia content annotation is crucial for Information Retrieval applications. However, the lack of sufficient labelled data restricts the potential of deep learning models in these areas. This research proposes a novel unsupervised approach to generate large-scale video annotation datasets, leveraging the vast amount of user-generated content on YouTube. By combining video segmentation and functional annotation, the method enables the creation of a large video dataset with detailed annotations. The developed pipeline is adaptable to various annotation tasks, and the generated dataset can be utilized for training machine learning models. The proposed pipeline is applied to a large-scale video dataset, resulting in a new collection of 1,125 videos with functional annotations, which is made available for public use.

The preservation of diversity in large ecosystems is a complex phenomenon that remains poorly understood. Recent theories suggest that diversity arises from the interplay of three key mechanisms: niche creation, niche expansion, and the shift of species into unoccupied ecological niches. This study investigates the interplay of these mechanisms in a simple model of competing species that can occupy multiple habitats. Our findings indicate that the model's behavior is influenced by the rate at which species can occupy new habitats. Specifically, we show that the model can exhibit a stable coexistence of species at a single point in parameter space, but that this stability is disrupted when species can occupy multiple habitats at a faster rate. Numerical simulations reveal that the model can also exhibit complex oscillatory behavior, characterized by periodic shifts between different species states. This behavior is similar to that observed in the Lotka-Volterra model, and can be understood in terms of the model's underlying dynamics.

Network vulnerability is a significant concern in contemporary research. This study employs a percolation model to investigate the resilience of a network against targeted attacks. Our approach involves simulating node removal through an avalanche, where an isolated power is gradually restored by reactivating a single node. We focus on a critical zone near the network's boundary, where the power dynamics exhibit chaotic behavior. Our findings reveal that the sensitivity of the power pattern to node removal is influenced by the distance from the network's center and can be leveraged to assess the network's structural properties.

To assess the depth of text comprehension, we've developed a dataset of 1,000 questions that require the reader to demonstrate a thorough understanding of the material. These open-ended questions are designed to be answered with evidence from the provided text and have been annotated to reflect the specific locations within the text where supporting information can be found. To evaluate the effectiveness of question answering models, we've created a new challenge that requires models to locate the correct evidence from the text and provide a well-supported answer to the question. Our experiments demonstrate that models struggle to meet the demands of this task, particularly when it comes to retrieving relevant information from the text.

A novel absorbing condition is introduced to address the challenges of wave propagation in unbounded domains. This condition combines elements of traditional perfectly matched layers and localized non-reflecting boundary conditions. By employing a simple, non-linear scaling factor, the proposed condition effectively transitions between different regimes, maintaining robust absorption performance across a range of wavenumber norms. The condition's flexibility is demonstrated in its ability to handle complex topographies, including scenarios with multiple scales and directions. Numerical experiments confirm the condition's efficacy in a wide range of applications, including scenarios with high-frequency waves and complex geometries.

We have developed a novel approach to study the fluid dynamics of multiple droplets by creating a platform that allows for the precise manipulation of droplet size, position, and movement. This flexible surface, made of a soft elastomer, can be deformed by the droplets themselves, enabling us to experimentally control the inter-droplet distances and interactions. Our experimental findings are supported by a theoretical model that accounts for the elasticity of the surface, and we have successfully replicated a range of complex phenomena, including droplet coalescence and fragmentation, by adjusting the surface properties. This research opens up new possibilities for exploring the behavior of multiple droplets on soft surfaces and holds potential applications in fields like chemical synthesis and biological research.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is a rapidly expanding network of interconnected devices, including sensors, actuators, and cameras, which are capable of exchanging data at any time. The increasing reliance on IoT technology in smart cities and industrial settings has led to a growing need for high-performance networks that can support Quality of Service (QoS) requirements. This paper presents a comprehensive review of existing QoS solutions for IoT networks, including the challenges and limitations of current approaches. We also explore the potential benefits of integrating advanced technologies like Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Blockchain in achieving QoS for IoT applications.

We've made a groundbreaking discovery in the protoplanetary disk of MWC 480, 
revealing a distinctive ring-like structure that extends 70 astronomical units 
and is characterized by a unique spiral pattern. This finding suggests the disk 
contains a developing planet with a mass of approximately 0.1 to 0.15 Jupiter masses, 
located at a distance of about 70 astronomical units. This marks the first time 
such a feature has been detected in a disk of this type and offers a unique 
opportunity to study the early stages of planet formation.

This paper introduces a novel distance metric, based on distances between the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of symmetric positive definite matrices, to quantify differences between probability density functions. The proposed distance has a significant advantage, allowing it to be zero if and only if the density functions are identical. The research further develops an algorithm to compute this distance efficiently and applies it to the analysis of financial risk. The authors examine the relationship between their approach and classic distance metrics, including Fisher information distance and Hellinger distance, and demonstrate its practical application using real-world and simulated data by comparing it with Wasserstein distance.

The integration of a hydrogen network offers a solution for managing the fluctuations in the supply of renewable energy. This study examines the potential of a large hydrogen storage system, capable of absorbing an entire country's renewable energy, and assesses its impact on the power grid. By converting excess energy into hydrogen and using it to generate electricity, the system can mitigate short-term fluctuations, but its ability to do so diminishes as it's converted back to electricity. To address this limitation, a time frame is proposed for the network's operation, with the option to store or generate electricity, rather than constantly switching between the two.

We have developed a new method to determine how the Sun's interior magnetic fields are oriented using measurements of travel time anisotropy. This method utilizes ray tracing to simulate seismic waves as if they travel through a magnetic field model, and it has been applied to the Sun's sub surface structure using data from the SOLO-D project. Our results show that the magnetic field orientation can be determined to within a 30-degree range, and that the strength of the magnetic field can be estimated to within a 50% margin. This method has been applied to the Sun's core and outer layers, and it has been used to study how the magnetic field changes with depth.

The generation of squeezed light is crucial for various quantum applications, including precision measurement, communication, and computation. In particular, this light is vital for achieving the quantum Cramer-Rao bound in interferometry. However, the production of this light is challenging due to the requirement of low-temperature optical cryostats. In this research, we present a novel approach to producing continuous-wave squeezed light at room temperature using a cavity-enhanced interaction between atomic vapor and an optical cavity. Our experiment involves using a cascaded process of optical parametric amplification to generate squeezed light, and we successfully produce a squeezing factor of -4.9(1) at 1530 nm. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility of generating high-squeezing-parameter squeezed light by using a cavity with a long length and a large mirror coating. Our method has the potential to produce high-quality squeezed light for various room-temperature quantum applications.

This paper addresses the challenge of finding the optimal control strategy to quickly move a drone from one location to another using the shortest possible time. To achieve this, we employ a geometric approach that involves using the Pontryagin Maximum Principle to find the necessary conditions for the minimum-time problem. We simplify the analysis by assuming a specific path and a given flight trajectory, which allows us to derive the required control input. The resulting control strategy is based on the concept of parallel transport in differential geometry.

This paper outlines the construction of a specific type of code known as the additive conjugacy code, which is derived from the permutation of subgroups within a finite field. We establish a direct relationship between this code and a previously established linear code, identifying the conditions under which this relationship holds. Additionally, the paper provides an in-depth analysis of the properties of the additive conjugacy code, including its ability to be extended and its dual properties. We also explore the scenario where this code is generated by a single element and derive a number of its key properties.

As a tenure-track assistant professor of physics at a small liberal arts college known as Mills College, I have encountered several unique challenges in my career. These difficulties stem from being a physicist in a predominantly undergraduate institution, where my college tends to hire very few other physicists. In this context, I have had to navigate the challenges of seeking out my professional community while working in a relatively isolated environment. In this article, I will share my experiences of finding and engaging with the broader physics community, particularly at a time when I am nearing the midpoint of my first tenure-track appointment. I will also explore the specific strategies I have used to overcome the obstacles I faced, offering insights that may be helpful to others who have similar experiences.

Using 1.7 fb^-1 of data from pp collisions at 7 TeV, researchers have analyzed W+Z production and its polarization effects. They discovered the W boson's polarization state in W to muon and electron pairs. The results showed polarization fractions of 0.683, 0.667, and 0.735 for left-handed, right-handed, and unknown states respectively. The polarization state of the W boson was consistent with standard model predictions.

The study of semileptonic B-meson decays into D-mesons can be used to investigate the twist-2 and twist-3 distribution amplitudes of the D-meson. This process involves a vector or axial-vector current interacting with a lepton, such as an electron or muon. The resulting decay spectrum is sensitive to the distribution amplitudes of the D-meson, making it a potential tool for studying their properties. In this work, we have calculated the decay spectrum of B-meson decays into D-mesons, taking into account the twist-2 and twist-3 distribution amplitudes of the D-meson, and have found that the decay of the B-meson into the D-meson is a promising process for studying the distribution amplitudes of the D-meson.

This paper introduces a novel method to calculate the eigenvalues of power hypergraphs, which is rooted in the eigenvalues of signed subgraphs derived from hypergraph subgraphs. This approach offers a systematic way to generate eigenvalues without requiring the entire hypergraph, and it is particularly useful for large-scale hypergraphs.

As the number of satellites in low Earth orbit mega-constellations rapidly increases, precise localisation and tracking become essential for collision avoidance and preventing satellite interference. To address this challenge, we investigate the feasibility of a cooperative localisation technique that leverages the timing signals broadcast by these satellites. By utilising a novel method, we can simultaneously determine the position, velocity, and timing errors of a satellite, enabling the estimation of its trajectory. This approach is demonstrated to be effective through simulations, which show that it can achieve high accuracy in localising satellites and even recover velocity information when no prior knowledge is available.

The transit timing variation of hot Jupiters is a valuable tool in understanding their migration history, yet many TTV signals remain unexplained. We have developed a new method to uncover these hidden signals using a deep learning approach. Our method, deep TTV, uses a deep neural network to identify patterns in transit timing data and can be applied to large datasets without preconceptions. We tested our method on simulated data and found that it can recover signals from planets with small semi-amplitude changes. We then applied our method to real data and discovered a TTV signal in the hot Jupiter WASP-12 b. Our results suggest that the planet's orbital decay is slowing down, consistent with tidal interaction between the planet and its host star. We also found that the amplitude of the signal is much larger than previously thought, indicating that WASP-12 b may be in a state of mutual influence. Our findings highlight the potential of our deep TTV method to uncover hidden signals in transit timing data.

In various fields of cosmic research, accurately measuring signal strength is a crucial task. This study presents a novel, data-driven calibration approach grounded in the principles of deep learning. The proposed method was tested using a simulated dataset of 20,000 galaxy spectra generated with the Prospector software. The results indicate that the deep learning technique surpasses established calibration methods, particularly in scenarios where the signal-to-noise ratio is low. Specifically, deep learning enhances mean absolute error by nearly 50% and standard deviation by 30% compared to traditional calibration methods. The study also found that incorporating a Gaussian Process regression model, which is a type of non-parametric regression, can further improve the deep learning results. The improved performance is attributed to the GP model's ability to capture subtle patterns in the data. The proposed calibration method is expected to yield significant benefits in real-world applications, particularly in scenarios where the signal is weak.

Given two equivariant vector bundles of equal rank with identical equivariant Chern classes over a GKM manifold with a finite group action, we demonstrate that their characteristic polynomials are identically matched, thereby establishing their equivalence.

We establish a prime number theorem for a specific subset of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms over the rational numbers, which are associated with the group $\mathrm{GL}_2$ and have finite slope. This theorem implies a prime number theorem for any given Dirichlet character. Furthermore, our findings extend Poincaré's work on arithmetic progressions, specifically for these forms. Additionally, our method can be applied to extend Poincaré's work to other arithmetic progressions.

In clinical trials with repeated measurements over time, mixed model repeated measures (MMRM) analysis is a common approach. However, treating time as categorical can lead to issues with model identifiability and make it difficult to assess trends in treatment effects. A new method, the generalized linear mixed model with a Poisson distribution (GLMMPD), is introduced to account for continuous time. This approach is validated through simulations and real-world data analysis, demonstrating its robustness and superiority to MMRM.

We introduce a novel algorithm for routing connected cars that leverages the crowd,  allowing individual cars to access real-time information about traffic conditions and make informed routing decisions. This approach is divided into two stages: a planning phase and a query phase. In the planning phase, a method for determining the optimal algorithm parameters is developed, taking into account the likelihood of queries and the benefits of accurate responses. Building upon existing research, a probabilistic model of the algorithm's performance is established, and the optimal algorithm parameters are determined using historical data. In the query phase, a new car arrives with its destination and queries the crowd for the best route, using the collected answers to update the algorithm parameters. Through this process, a probabilistic model of the algorithm's performance is continuously refined, allowing for more accurate queries over time. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, showing that it can significantly reduce travel times and emissions while minimizing the need for queries.

Recent studies have shown that neural networks trained with small initial weights tend to converge to flat-minima, which can enhance their generalization capabilities. However, achieving flat-minima optimization is challenging due to the difficulty of finding good initial weights. To address this issue, we introduce a novel initialisation method that leverages the properties of complex networks to identify suitable initial weights. Our experiments on various tasks, including image classification and graph learning, confirm that this method can effectively initialise flat-minima and improve the model's generalisation performance.

This paper presents a novel approach to integrating diode-based parametric frequency
selective limiters into photonic radio-frequency filters. The design allows for
optical frequency division and enables the transfer of power from a specific
diode load to a specific filter port, effectively suppressing unwanted signals
at the same frequency but passing through signals at different frequencies. The
proposed system's effectiveness in suppressing electromagnetic interference in
radios is demonstrated through a practical example, showcasing the benefits of
this design.

This study explores the dynamics of an SIR model applied to an untraceable population, focusing on the factors influencing disease propagation and the likelihood of the disease persisting within the population. Through a combination of analytical and numerical methods, we determine the conditions necessary for the disease to continue spreading, and calculate the threshold for reproduction that determines the disease's potential impact. Additionally, we examine how increased awareness among the population can hinder the disease's spread, and investigate the critical relationships between the rate of reproduction, population awareness, and the disease's potential impact.

We introduce a novel approach to incorporating multiple words within a single neural network component, which is applied to the task of text classification. By leveraging distributed representations of words and phrases as input to a neural network, we demonstrate improved performance in text classification tasks. Specifically, our method yields state-of-the-art results for identifying hate speech and semantic similarity between text passages.

We consider a random geometric graph with n vertices and an edge probability that decays as n to the power of -k, with k being the order of the graph. We establish that the expected number of components of order k in this graph converges to a fixed value as n becomes very large. Furthermore, we prove that the variance associated with this number also converges to a fixed value multiple of the square of the expected number, by demonstrating that the variance is essentially equivalent to the product of two independent indicator functions. This is achieved by examining the properties of a random vector representing the presence or absence of components in a specific order in a random geometric graph with a fixed vertex set.

We have developed a numerical method to calculate equilibrium configurations of rotating stars, which employs a Lagrangian approach to maintain the physical relationships between the fluid and the grid. Our method, based on an Eulerian-Lagrangian scheme, uses a Poisson solver and an ODE solver to find the solutions, and is suitable for use in general relativity frameworks. We tested our method with simulations of rotating neutron stars and found that it produces accurate results, comparable to an Eulerian approach, within a Lagrangian framework.

This paper explores the generalized Lema\^{\i}tre-Tolman-Bondi spacetime, which is a solution to Einstein's gravitational field equations incorporating a perfect fluid source with anisotropic pressure. Notably, this spacetime is a generalization of the LTB spacetime, which is itself a solution. We derive key properties of the GLTB spacetime, including its physical characteristics, conserved quantities, and energy conditions. Our findings demonstrate that the GLTB spacetime shares several properties with the LTB spacetime, such as the mass function and the Ricci scalar.

We have identified a large collection of $3 \times 3$ multipartite orthogonal quantum states, specifically $12$ in total, that are strongly nonlocal. This set, consisting of $4$ entangled states, $6$ GHZ-like states, and $2$ W-like states, serves as a local description for each state. The presence of such a set is significant in the context of multipartite quantum games, as it reveals the local weakness of these games.

The escalating demand for identifying and categorizing web user behavior poses significant challenges for current information extraction techniques. To address this issue, we have developed a novel approach for extracting and categorizing web user navigation patterns. This method involves the use of a hybrid knowledge base, comprising a semantic network and a classification tree, to analyze and classify user navigation patterns. By leveraging the semantic network, we can pinpoint the underlying intentions behind users' actions, such as visit, search, or search and visit. Meanwhile, the classification tree enables us to classify user navigation patterns into distinct categories, such as users searching for information, accessing specific content, or engaging in malicious behavior. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we have conducted a comprehensive evaluation using a substantial dataset of web user navigation patterns.

A novel reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) design is introduced that leverages the principles of metasurves to create a transmissive RIS with the capability to manipulate both the amplitude and phase of transmitted signals. This metasurface-based RIS is capable of transmitting wireless signals with high efficiency, making it an energy-friendly alternative to traditional RIS. A comprehensive analysis of the RIS's impact on wireless communication systems is conducted, focusing on its performance in single-input single-output (SISO) and multiple-input single-output (MISO) systems. Theoretical models are developed to quantify the maximum achievable signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in SISO and MISO systems, as well as to determine the maximum transmission power of the RIS. These results are further validated through numerical simulations that demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed RIS design.

Offline reinforcement learning involves training an agent on a pre-recorded dataset
without interaction with the environment.  This approach is appealing due to its
ability to reduce costs, but it poses a challenge in formulating a suitable
objective function that can adapt to diverse environments.  A new method, called
Deep Variational Policy Search with an Information Bottleneck, is proposed to
overcome this challenge by combining an information-theoretic regularization with
a variational objective function to achieve robustness to environmental variations.
  The proposed method is demonstrated through experiments on MuJoCo benchmarks,
which show that it outperforms existing offline RL methods, including those that use
behavior cloning and maximum entropy techniques.

We demonstrate that some of the free theorem consequences derived from the Berrondarou, Pouly, and Sozeau free theorems [6] can also be obtained through a new type of unification in intensional type theory, without requiring specific additional axioms. Furthermore, we show that these additional consequences, including the free theorem for the composition of polymorphic functions with polymorphic functions of simpler type, cannot be deduced from the initial postulates.

We've identified a new galaxy at redshift z=0.940 that's located at RA=04h 37m 21.8s, Dec=+24° 56' 06" with a 1.5 arcmin diameter. This newly discovered galaxy was found through the use of a spectrograph in a 1.5 hour observation. We've confirmed the galaxy's distance from Earth using a spectrum that shows redshifted hydrogen and oxygen light. We've estimated the galaxy's distance using a spectrum that shows redshifted hydrogen light, which puts it 7.7 billion parsecs away. We've also estimated the galaxy's mass using a spectrum that shows redshifted hydrogen light, which puts it at 1.4 x 10^10 solar masses. This newly discovered galaxy is part of a group of galaxies that are likely to be gravitationally bound together.

This work explores the three-body problem in its most general form, with the aim of identifying systematic relationships among solutions. These relationships are referred to as generalised syzygies. A novel approach to finding solutions to the three-body problem is presented, which involves initially identifying a set of solutions that satisfy certain conditions, and then using these solutions to determine additional solutions. This method is used to discover numerous novel solutions to the three-body problem. Furthermore, the study reveals that the systematic relationships among solutions can be utilised to calculate the mass ratios of the particles in solutions to a high degree of accuracy.

Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) measures the lifespan of fluorescent molecules at each point in an image, offering insights into the energy states and chemical environments of these molecules. This information can be used to create detailed images of biological tissues, which can be particularly helpful in studying diseases and developing new treatments. However, traditional FLIM systems often require expensive and complex optical components, such as high-speed cameras and sophisticated light sources. This research presents a new, simplified FLIM system that uses a single commercial camera and a single, affordable light source to capture and analyze the fluorescence patterns at each image point. By analyzing the data from these images, the researchers can determine the energy states of the molecules and create detailed, high-resolution images of the tissues under study. This new approach has the potential to make FLIM a more accessible and affordable tool for researchers and clinicians.

Personalized product search relies heavily on effective user preference modeling.
To this end, we introduce a novel approach that integrates both explicit and
implicit user-item interactions, including ratings, clicks, and orderings, into a
unified representation. This is achieved by treating ratings as a continuous
version of click events and orderings as a more refined indication of
similarity. We then use a neural network to learn the preferences of users and
item attributes, which are represented as graphs. This approach is tested on a
large dataset of Amazon Recommandations and results show significant
improvements over existing methods.

Graph embedding techniques have gained significant attention in graph mining tasks.  However, the resulting embeddings often lack stability, hindering their applicability in downstream tasks.  To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that incorporates adversarial learning to enhance the stability of embeddings.  Our method, called GraphAdversarial, is a general framework that can be applied to various graph embedding tasks.  We validate the efficacy of our method through experiments on node classification, clustering, and link prediction tasks, demonstrating its superiority over existing state-of-the-art baselines.

In massive machine-type communications, grant-free access has proven to be an effective method, enabling numerous devices to transmit data simultaneously in a random access channel without the need for specific permission. This approach is beneficial for applications such as remote sensing, but it also poses significant detection challenges for the base station. To address this issue, we propose a novel deep learning-based method that enables the base station to simultaneously detect information symbols from multiple users, even when their signals are severely degraded by noise. Our approach involves training a deep neural network to jointly detect signals from multiple users, using complex-valued data and leveraging the inherent sparsity of the channel to enhance its performance. Simulation results demonstrate that this method outperforms traditional methods, particularly in difficult channel conditions.

In the context of compressed sensing, we examine the problem of recovering a sparse signal from a set of noisy measurements, which are linear combinations of the signal with a matrix that is randomly generated. We investigate the conditions under which the signal can be accurately recovered with near-optimal precision, which has been a topic of extensive research. Our study focuses on the specific scenario where the signal is estimated using a convex optimization method, which has been shown to provide a solution that is close to optimal in certain conditions. We derive a precise estimate of the conditions under which this solution is guaranteed to be optimal, which significantly improves upon previous results and provides a more accurate understanding of the requirements for optimal recovery. Our work also reveals a new set of conditions under which the solution is guaranteed to be optimal, which are independent of the signal-to-noise ratio and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the requirements for optimal recovery.

Deep neural networks have been found to excel in a variety of tasks, but their performance is often hindered by a lack of generalizability and sensitivity to domain shifts. To address this issue, researchers have proposed the use of domain adaptation and generalization methods, which involve training models on non-target domains to improve performance on target domains. However, these approaches often overlook the potential of data augmentation, a technique that can enhance model performance. This study investigates the effectiveness of data augmentation, particularly random cropping and flipping, in improving domain adaptation and generalization performance. The results show that data augmentation can significantly improve model performance, and a combination of domain adaptation and generalization techniques can outperform state-of-the-art methods, even without the use of adversarial techniques.
This paper demonstrates that in the Jordan ring of 2x2 self-adjoint matrices over any field, all 2-local inner derivations can be expressed as derivations.

Berry's phase, a distinctive geometric effect in adiabatic processes, has garnered significant attention in both fundamental and applied physics. Initially introduced in the context of quantum mechanics, Berry's phase has since been generalized to various physical systems, including non-relativistic particles, photons, and other entities. This review aims to provide an in-depth exploration of the geometric phase, focusing on its underlying geometric structure and evolution in different physical systems. The review covers the historical development of the geometric phase concept, its connections to geometric structures, and its applications in physical systems, including those with non-Abelian gauge symmetries. The discussion also extends to experimental realizations of the geometric phase, its role in quantum computing, and its broader implications in modern physics.

We investigate the dynamics of compacton matter waves in a binary mixture of Bose-Einstein condensates confined within an optical lattice, employing a generalized discrete second-order nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a time-dependent coefficient. This model is relevant to the study of atomic dark solitons in a binary Bose-Einstein condensate system, and its properties are analyzed using the method of mathematical moments. We find that the existence and stability of compacton matter waves are contingent upon the strength of the confining potential and the strength of the interaction between the two boson components. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the compacton matter waves can be stabilized through confinement and interaction, and we present numerical simulations to illustrate these findings.

We investigate the heavy-quark spin symmetry (HQSS) in the molecular states of charmed and bottom baryons, specifically $B_{c}\Lambda_{c}$ and $\Lambda_{Q}\Lambda_{Q}$. We then apply the molecular non-relativistic QCD (MNRQCD) approach to calculate the molecular states of $B_{c}\Lambda_{c}$ and $\Lambda_{Q}\Lambda_{Q}$. Our results show that the spin-1 and spin-2 states of $B_{c}\Lambda_{c}$ and $\Lambda_{Q}\Lambda_{Q}$ are consistent with the experimental data of $P_{c}(4440)^{+}$ and $P_{b}(6090)^{+}$, respectively. We also find that the spin-0 state of $P_{b}(6090)^{+}$ is consistent with the experimental data of $P_{b}(6090)^{+}$, which indicates that the heavy-quark spin symmetry plays a significant role in the HQET charmonium-like and bottomonium-like molecular pentaquark states.

This paper demonstrates the existence of a smooth approximation for a continuous function f when it belongs to a specific space, and provides a quantitative expression for this approximation. The research then applies this concept to a particular function space, deriving an original inequality in the process.

We investigate the potential of detecting a specific type of particle, namely axion-like particles that interact with the standard model gauge bosons, using a particular process that occurs in proton-proton collisions. This process, known as the Drell-Yan process, can be used to search for these particles by analyzing the characteristics of the particles produced in the collision. We have developed a method to estimate the sensitivity of the Large Hadron Collider in detecting these particles, taking into account the limitations imposed by the collision conditions and the sensitivity of the detectors. We have also considered the effects of the particles' interactions with the particles produced in the collision and the limitations imposed by the collision conditions and the sensitivity of the detectors.

This research introduces a novel hardware-software collaboration technique that enables general-purpose processors to efficiently execute complex tasks typically handled by dedicated accelerators. By utilizing this approach, we can successfully run tasks like convolutional neural network inference and matrix multiplication on standard CPUs, achieving performance levels comparable to those of high-end FPGAs.

Deep learning techniques have revolutionized the field of computer vision, 
with pre-trained networks from large image datasets providing valuable features 
that can be leveraged in various applications. However, the extraction of 
deep semantic features from 3D point clouds remains a complex task, 
especially in scenarios where data is limited. This research proposes a novel 
approach to extract deep semantic features from 3D point clouds using a 
two-stage process. The first stage involves the use of a pre-trained CNN to 
extract image features from RGB-D images, which are then used to predict the 
3D semantic labels of the input point clouds. The second stage utilizes a 
U-Net to predict the 3D voxel labels of the input point clouds, with the 
labels serving as a supervisory signal to train the U-Net. The proposed 
method demonstrates promising results on the KITTI 3D semantic segmentation 
benchmark, with the code available for public access.

This study establishes the existence of a solution to a quasi-linear elliptic system presented in [23], utilizing the theory of monotone operators and the fixed point theorem. Furthermore, we introduce an innovative approach to prove the uniqueness of the solution.

Recurrent neural networks are capable of modeling long-term dependencies, but training them for such tasks can be challenging due to vanishing or exploding gradients. To address this issue, researchers have developed various techniques to control the gradient variability. However, these methods often require significant modifications to the network architecture or incur high computational costs. In contrast, this paper proposes a straightforward approach to training recurrent neural networks for natural language processing tasks by incorporating pre-normalization. The proposed method is effective in reducing the gradient normalization requirement, allowing it to handle long-term dependencies during language modeling and machine translation tasks. The results demonstrate that pre-normalization achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art models while offering a more efficient and cost-effective solution.

We present a novel approach to model-based planning for Markov Decision Processes, which ensures that the resulting policies yield a steady-state distribution. This approach is applicable to both discounted and infinite horizon settings and can be used to create policies that achieve a specified steady-state distribution. Our method is based on converting the MDP into a Partially Observable Markov Process, which enables the use of a dynamic programming algorithm to construct a steady-state recognition function. This recognition function can then be used to develop a control policy that achieves the desired steady-state distribution. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through experiments in the context of reinforcement learning and active learning.

We have developed a groundbreaking approach to creating an extremely intense attosecond electron bunch using a laser-based electron bunch compressor. By leveraging a laser-induced phase modulation technique, we can produce an attosecond electron bunch with a high polarization efficiency of over 99%, while maintaining a consistent beam profile. Our novel method utilizes a laser with a specific intensity distribution, enabling both compression and polarization of the electron bunch simultaneously. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach using 3D particle-in-cell simulations and an analytical model, and show that it can be integrated into existing linear accelerators to produce an attosecond electron bunch with a high charge and low emittance.

The concept of vital scalar field was first introduced by Pierre Teilhard de Chambret in 1928, suggesting a gradual increase in complexity throughout the universe. This idea is being explored as a potential explanation for the emergence of life on Earth. Our research aims to demonstrate that the scalar field is linked to the entropy of the universe, which in turn drives the increase in complexity. This is achieved by analyzing the scalar field in relation to the expansion of the universe and its connection to the emergence of life on Earth. Our findings indicate that the scalar field is responsible for the increase in complexity, providing a natural explanation for the emergence of life. This is supported by the observation that the scalar field is correlated with the emergence of life at different stages, and that it is driving the increase in complexity throughout the universe.

To build effective Science, Technology, and Innovation ecosystems, it's crucial that policymakers have accurate and comprehensive research data at their disposal. However, current access to research findings is often restricted, leaving a gap in the information needed for informed decision making. To bridge this gap, a novel dataset has been developed, providing a detailed picture of research output and access policies across 81 countries from 2015 to 2020. The dataset reveals that the majority of research is locked behind paywalls, with a notable concentration in the fields of health, environmental science, and engineering. The study's findings suggest that the main drivers behind restricted access are the cost of licenses, the speed of access, and the geographic limitations. The research also highlights the disparities in access policies among countries and the need for more transparent and accessible publishing practices within the academic community.

The widespread adoption of smartphones has led to the development of numerous mobile applications, which are often vulnerable to side-channel attacks. Despite the growing threat of side-channel exploits, there is a lack of comprehensive tools to detect them. This study introduces a novel approach to automatically identify side-channel vulnerabilities in Android applications. Leveraging a large dataset of real-world side-channel vulnerabilities, our method employs a deep learning model to classify side-channel and non-side-channel code snippets. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our technique in detecting side-channel vulnerabilities with high accuracy.

This research examines the transaction patterns of Ethereum accounts, focusing on self-similar accounts, which are identified by their transactions being similar to the overall network's activity. We analyze the accounts' transactions using network features, which are calculated based on their connections, and distinguish self-similar accounts based on their calculated features. Our study reveals that self-similar accounts are concentrated among contract accounts, and their transaction patterns differ from those of other account types. Additionally, we find that the self-similar accounts' network features exhibit distinct characteristics compared to other account types.

We have conducted a study on the impact of illumination on a two-dimensional electron system at the interface of LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ in a magnetic field, observing a significant decrease in sheet resistance. This decrease is accompanied by an increase in the Hall coefficient and a narrowing of the Hall gap. We attribute these changes to the generation of electron-hole pairs by the laser, which increases the electron density and reduces the electron mobility due to increased scattering. Our findings indicate that the mobility of electrons in this system is influenced by the number of electrons rather than the magnetic field strength. This suggests that the mobility is limited by the interface itself rather than by the magnetic field.

BV logic extends Intuitionistic Propositional Logic with two additional connectives,
providing a natural framework for formalizing proofs. This logic facilitates the
construction of a Kripke semantics-based proof system that is sound and complete,
and its decision problem is complexity-classified as co-2EXPTIME-complete.

A unified approach is provided for the pentagon identity of the quantum dilogarithm functions at all square roots of -1. The proof relies on the star-triangle relation of the Ising lattice model and involves a geometric transformation of the pentagon identity of the $\mathbb{F}_1$ affine symmetric function theory.

We have developed a novel approach to estimate photometric redshifts using a combination of deep learning and machine learning techniques. Our method, which utilizes a convolutional neural network, can accurately predict redshifts for a diverse set of galaxies. We have tested our approach on the Hubble Space Telescope's Cosmic Assembly Near-infrared Deep Survey Field data, achieving a high accuracy of 0.027 magnitudes when compared to spectroscopic redshifts. Our method also allows for the identification of outliers and the estimation of uncertainty in redshifts. Furthermore, we have successfully applied our approach to the Frontier Fields data, obtaining reliable redshifts for 80% of galaxies. Our method has also been used to identify highly magnified galaxies in these fields, including a galaxy with a magnification of 30 and a redshift of 2.1.

This research explores the potential of Gaussian Process emulators to enhance the efficiency of complex computer models. By combining the principles of Bayesian analysis and statistical emulators, this method offers a valuable tool for computer experiments. The study presents a new approach to selecting the most effective emulator models through the development of a novel metric. By comparing the results of this metric to traditional methods, such as the maximum likelihood criterion, this paper evaluates the performance of various emulators under different computer models. The research also examines the impact of model complexity on prediction accuracy and discusses the limitations of the maximum likelihood criterion. Ultimately, this paper proposes a new strategy for selecting the optimal emulator model and demonstrates its effectiveness through a series of case studies involving a range of complex computer models.

We have developed a novel approach to calculate the exact ground state energy of a two-electron system using the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) method. By optimizing the bond dimension and fine-tuning the optimization algorithm, we successfully obtained the ground state energy with minimal truncation errors. Our method involves calculating the full ground state wavefunction and then evaluating any desired property using this wavefunction. We have implemented the quantum Monte Carlo density matrix renormalization group (QC-DMRG) method using the full spectrum projection algorithm to calculate the ground state wavefunction in a basis of Slater determinants. Our results show that the optimal bond dimension for two-electron systems is 16, and we have achieved an accuracy of 10^-9 for the ground state energy. We have also demonstrated the accuracy of our method by comparing it with the exact solution for the H3 system and with the results from other popular quantum chemistry methods.

We investigate the effects of a non-Abelian $SU(2)_X$ symmetry in the muon's anomalous magnetic moment and the $\mu \to e$ gamma transition. This research reveals that a specific model with a non-Abelian $SU(2)_X$ can accommodate the observed muon magnetic moment while imposing constraints on the muon electron transition via the GIM mechanism.

A novel machine learning-based approach is proposed to efficiently replicate complex high-resolution coastal and ocean models, which are crucial for predicting climate change impacts. The method involves developing a simplified model that captures the essential dynamics of the high-resolution model, thereby facilitating the analysis of various climate scenarios. The performance of the proposed model is evaluated against two high-resolution models, MIKE FLOOD and SWAN, which are used to simulate flood and wave patterns in coastal regions. The results indicate that the model accurately predicts long-term trends and seasonal fluctuations in the high-resolution models, while also being computationally efficient.

We are releasing a comprehensive end-to-end analysis pipeline for cosmic microwave background (CMB) experiments, optimized for small-scale radio frequency interferometry (RFI) instruments. This Python-based pipeline, built with the widely used HEALPix spatial grid, is designed to quickly process maps across various frequencies and enable real-time analysis. To facilitate the CMB community's research, the pipeline is openly accessible, including its associated code, documentation, and an interactive web-based tutorial.

We investigate a simplified model of Turing instability, comprising two interconnected components, each comprising a single variable, coupled via linear interaction and governed by a finite-dimensional space and discrete time constraints. The linear interaction is represented by a symmetric matrix with real values. The Turing instability phenomenon is characterized by the emergence of unstable patterns in space, with uniform time consistency. We demonstrate that this phenomenon can be expressed as the non-negativity of a specific parameter-dependent matrix, with the parameter set belonging to a defined algebraic space. The instability patterns in question are represented by the eigenvectors of this matrix, with the corresponding eigenvalues indicating their respective stability properties. We further establish that these eigenvectors exhibit exponential growth or decay as the parameter value approaches its instability threshold.

We introduce a phantom field to standard pure Yang-Mills theory, resulting in a theory that exhibits quantum cancellation, and corresponds to a modified version of the quantum effective action for the theory. This theory is then shown to be renormalizable in the context of dimensional regularization with anti-$\epsilon$-rotation across the duality axis.

We have developed a comprehensive model to predict and analyze the polarization characteristics of GaAs/AlGaAs nanowires through photoluminescence experiments. Our model takes into account the spontaneous and piezoelectric polarization effects, allowing for the simulation of radiative recombination rates and resulting polarization behaviors. By comparing our model to experimental data, we have successfully replicated the polarization transition observed in the nanowires and identified the primary factor driving this phenomenon as the piezoelectric polarization. Furthermore, our model has been utilized to investigate the influence of the nanowire's radius and the core/middle interface on the polarization behavior.

In multi-issue negotiations, an opponent's priority order for individual issues is crucial information for the other party to make informed decisions. This knowledge can be used to predict potential outcomes and negotiate more effectively. Our research presents a method to infer an opponent's priority order by analyzing dialogue transcripts from previous negotiations. We've developed a neural network model that uses these transcripts as input to predict the opponent's priorities, which we've tested on data from real-world negotiations. Our experiments show that our model can accurately infer an opponent's priorities, even when their own position is unknown.

In the context of braneworlds, we explore the dynamics of string-like objects within the framework of fluxbrane black holes in a two-dimensional AdS space. The AdS geometry is generated by introducing a dynamical string tension at the brane, which also serves to confine strings and matter. The presence of a massive bulk scalar field leads to a unique black hole solution, and we examine its thermodynamic properties. Furthermore, we investigate the behavior of massive string-like worldlines within this framework and derive the corresponding equations of motion.

In online field experiments, researchers often deliberately distribute treatments across various characteristics to ensure equal treatment groups, a process known as covariate balancing. This balancing approach is now being explored for use in online covariate adjustment, a technique used to reduce bias in treatment estimators. This balancing approach can be incorporated into online covariate adjustment through a method called balancing stepwise marginal designs. These designs achieve balanced covariate distributions at each step, allowing for effective covariate adjustment. We propose a new algorithm for generating these designs and demonstrate its performance through simulations. We also apply our method to data from a COVID-19 vaccine trial, showing how it can be used to make informed decisions based on interim results.

A theoretical study of the (001)-Si/(001)-gamma-Al2O3 heterointerface was conducted, revealing that the interface is stable and free of defects. The calculations show that the interface is characterized by silicon atoms in a tetrahedral environment with four bonds to oxygen atoms, and aluminum atoms in a pentagonal environment with five bonds to silicon and oxygen atoms, including one or two bonds to the silicon atoms. The interface is found to be neutral, with a total charge of zero, and the atoms at the interface are found to be in a neutral state, with a total charge of zero. The calculations also show that the interface is stable and does not exhibit any defects, and the atoms at the interface are found to be in a neutral state, with a total charge of zero.

This research explores the application of numerical and graphical techniques to approximate the functional relationships underlying Black Hole physics within the four-dimensional axion-dilaton system, utilizing the connection between phase portraits and phase diagrams as a foundation.

A comprehensive dataset of 1,000 shipping containers has been compiled and made available for the shipping industry to develop and test advanced algorithms that address the complex challenges of container management. This data set was created in response to the container crisis that emerged in the late 2010s, resulting from a perfect storm of factors including a surge in container demand, supply chain bottlenecks, and the implementation of the Suez canal expansion project.
